newsitem.title: USA: Carville and Matalin appear in election night beer ads.
newsitem.headline: Carville and Matalin appear in election night beer ads.

text.p: James Carville and Mary Matalin, the married political consultants from opposing political camps, will spar head-to-head as marital combatants in Heineken beer commercals airing Tuesday during election night coverage.
The ads are part of the "Heard over a Heineken" campaign that New York agency Wells Rich Greene BDDP created for the Dutch brewer.

Like the other ads in the series, the Carville/Matalin spots are supposed to feature "authentic" conversation that attest to Heineken's authenticity as a beer brand. The ad agency that handled the commercial, though, admitted that the lines were taken partially from a script, with some ad-libbing by the political consultants during shootings.

The three television commercials take place in the bedroom, bathroom and living room of Carville and Matalin's Washington, D.C. home, where they are heard sparring over politics. There are no direct shots of the political couple, only-out-of-focus sequences that carry their conversation as a voice over.

One spot shows a blue-jeaned Carville, from the waste down, doing a victory dance in the living room in front of a chagrined Matalin. Shot before the election, the spots appear to presume a Democratic victory. "V-I-C-T-O-R-Y, victory that is our cry," Carville sings. "You are the biggest jerk," Matalin says.

In another of the ads, Carville reads a newspaper story suggesting he might run for president. Matalin says, "That writer is worse than a Democrat, he's an idiot." One other ad has Matalin, the Republican pundit, talking favourably of Bob Dole, while Carville, the Democrat, says supportive things about President Clinton. The scene takes place in their bedroom.

The ads were set to appear only on election night, on spots in the biggest television markets. The top-rated stations in each local market were tapped during the time when election results were scheduled.
The spots were not being aired on NBC stations, since Matalin and Carville both do political commentary for the network.

The high-profile political couple has appeared in consumer product commercials in the past. They were featured in a widely used American Express print ad that ran in many magazines and featured items they bought using their charge cards.
